transcript: Chapter 33. Kiva. The Week's Crossing. The printer's boy came up Key Street at five on Thursday morning, with a canvas bag on his hip and a stack of pages under his arm, and he was knocking at every door that had a light in it. Kiva heard him from the loft. She had been awake since four, lying on her back by the north window, with her right hand on her chest, because the blisters across her knuckles had come up in the night, as Ask had said they would, and had woken her with their own small heat. She heard the knocking go along the street toward the company's office, and stop, and come back. Then she heard Quiller's voice below, cross and thick with sleep, and the boy's voice answering, high and patient. Every catcher, the marshal says, everyone in the town, it's paid for. She got up and went down the outside stair in her coat, with her boots unlaced. The boy was on the step of the chandelier, with Quiller in the doorway above him in his nightshirt. He was perhaps twelve, with ink on both thumbs. When he saw Kiva on the stair, he looked at the linen on her right hand, and then at her face, and held out a page without being asked. You're the meridian one, he said. Mr. Tregear said there'd be one with the bound hand. He said give it to her first if she's up. She took it in her left hand. It was one sheet, printed on both sides, still faintly damp, and the ink smelled of oil. Across the head of it, above the title, there was a line in a heavier type than the rest. After D. Penhale, catcher, the Saltmere Company, at Mallow Creek, the sixteenth of the third month, 2681, who went in by the book. Under it, smaller, was the title she had seen in the marshal's own hand, on a wharf at home. On a thing that folds from the far edge. The marshal's page. Then came the page itself, which was short. Make the thing carry its sheet uphill, if it will. If it will not, put weight on the far edge. The far edge belongs to the second, as a place, and not to the corner hand. Somebody watches the far end of the thing, all through the slack, even while the slack holds. The book is written for a sheet. That was all. It did not say a stow anywhere, or a sleeve. It did not need to. Anybody who had stood on the causeway yesterday would read sheet, and see the other thing. Mr. Tregear said it himself, said the boy. All night. He knew Mr. Penhall's father. He shifted the bag on his hip. I've two hundred to do before six, miss. The vans and the company yard and the beats. Go on then, said Kiva. Thank you. He went off down the street at a trot. Quilla looked at the page in her hand, over the top of his spectacles. And then he took the second copy the boy had left on his step, and went back inside without a word, and shut the door. Kiva stood in the grey street and read it again. She did not cry. She had thought on the cart yesterday that she might, sometime. And had found it was not that kind of thing. It was a page that had been held back, in case it was wrong. And it was out now with a dead man's name at the top. And every catcher on the coast would have it in a pocket by breakfast. She folded it in four and put it inside her coat, against her ribs, where the disc was. Ivy came up the street at half past five, with Kiva's sheets under her arm, tied in their tape. She had not slept. It was in her face and in the way she walked, square and steady and a little too carefully, as people walk who have been up all night and mean to go on being up. She stopped at the foot of Quiller's stair and held the bundle out. Everyone copied, she said. Twice. One for Yeo and one for me. I've read them to the closing cruise officer already. I'll read them to the crew at six, before the boats. She looked at the marshal's page showing at the edge of Kiva's coat. You've had that. Five minutes ago. So have I. The boy came to the company yard first. Ivy's square dark hands were empty now, and she put them in her pockets. Yeo said to tell you two things. She wants your columns for every crew she has, not mine only. And she wants to know who taught you to keep a second sheet, because she means to have a second on every stow from now to the autumn, and she doesn't know where to find one. Pike, said Kiva. Greywater's catcher. He let me watch him. Then she'll talk to Pike. Ivy nodded once. She said, if you'd stand it, she'd like you on the company yard one evening, before you go home, to tell the crews the far edge, in your own words, not the marshal's, yours. She half turned to go. I said you'd say no if it was a lane night. She said, then not a lane night. Tell her yes, said Kiva. Not a lane night. Ivy went away down Key Street toward the low town and the company yard, where the vans were. Kiva stood at the foot of the stair with her own sheets under her arm, which smelled faintly now of the company's tar and somebody else's lamp, and found she did not mind it. Ask held her left hand, at seven, by the north window, for two minutes by his watch. The loft was full of people dressing. Haldin License was up at the south end, where Pettit was reading something aloud off a slip of paper, in a voice too low to carry. Old Four was arguing about who had taken whose boots. Selka Dre sat on the next bed to Sevens, with both feet on the floor, lacing a boot, and did not look round. Prue was on her own bed, with her hands held up in front of her in their ten little linen caps, waiting her turn. Perrin was sitting very upright on the end of his, in his shirt, with the strapping showing under it, being careful not to breathe. Ask Let Go Warm, he said. Four mornings. Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and today. He wrote it on the card against the window frame. Thursday's come, that's what I said, soonest. Oh no. Then I'll say the price, as I said I would. He did not sit down. He looked at her over his spectacles, and his voice did not change at all. The fifth went to a hand below the elbow, and sulked three nights. The sixth went to the elbow, with an ache in the joint, and sulked four. I think the seventh goes past the elbow. An inch, maybe two. I think it sulks five nights, and I'll not be surprised by six. He put the pen in his pocket. That's the hand. Here's the other thing, and it isn't the hand at all. It's the calendar. One in seven days. If you go today, the next is Thursday week. If you go Saturday, the next is the Saturday after. There's no crossing between. Whatever's on fire. He did not say Wednesday. He did not need to. Everybody within three beds of the window knew what Wednesday was. Dre's hands had stopped on her bootlace. Kiva sat on the edge of her bed with the hand in her lap. She had been thinking about it since the cart yesterday, coming back along the causeway with the longshore, going under brown water, and Bridie Hebden's legs white under a sheet in the tent behind them. She had thought about it in the printer's street at five, and on the stair with Ivy. She had not said it to anybody, because nobody had asked, and because she had wanted to be sure it was hers before she said it. On Wednesday, at nine minutes past six, if two people and a sealed paper were right, the basin would go still for twenty minutes. Somewhere in it, if anybody asked her, she would be calling a thing that three people did, catch and carry and plant, with a count that was not hers. And if one of the three failed, there was exactly one thing in her certificate that could stand in the gap, which was a crossing, on a sanctioned mast, read by the office's reader, one in seven days. Nobody had asked her for Wednesday. That was the point. If somebody asked on Tuesday, she wanted to be able to say yes without asking anybody to write a new line in a ledger. It's not for this week, she said. Perrin looked up from the end of his bed. He was the captain. He was entitled to ask. And he did. Not wanted in the lane. Not in the lane. Not today. Nor Friday. Nor Saturday. She found she could say it quite plainly. It's the week's crossing. I'd like to keep it for Wednesday. If nobody wants it on Wednesday, I'll have kept it for nothing, and that's all right. But if I spend it on a lane, I can't have it back. You'll fight Saturday on one door, said Perrin. Whoever we draw. I'll fight every day on one door. I've done it before. He looked at her for a long moment, with his big hands on his knees, and his face going the colour it went when he was thinking very hard. Then he nodded. Then it's the captain's as well, he said. Not wanted in the lane. I'll say so, if anybody asks. And they will. Ask had not moved. I've said the price once now, he said, for a crossing nobody's going to make. I'll say it again on Saturday morning, at this window, in case anybody's changed their mind by then. He looked at her steadily. Twice for nothing is cheaper than once too late. Put that in your book, on the right. I will. Beside her, Dre finished lacing her boot. She pulled the knot tight and stood up, and went down the room toward the stair. And she did not say anything, and she did not look at anybody. But Kiva saw her pause at the head of the stair for a moment, with her hand on the post, as a person pauses who has heard a figure that changes a sum. Ask turned to Perrin. He did not say anything first. He sat down on the bed beside him, which made Perrin go rigid, and he put two fingers flat on the strapping over the seventh rib on the left side, very lightly, and held them there. Breathe in, he said. Perrin breathed in, or did not get very far. Out, Ask moved his fingers an inch. Again. He listened to something, or seemed to. Then he took his fingers away and looked at the strapping itself, at the place over the rib where the linen had been wound on Tuesday at two. One edge of it had pulled. It had pulled hard enough to fold back on itself, and a crease ran across it like a seam. When did you lift? Perrin went scarlet, said Ask. Perrin went scarlet from the collar up. It was the first time Kiva had ever seen him go the colour that Prue went. I didn't, he began, and stopped, because Ask was looking at him over his spectacles with no expression whatever. At the spur, he said. Yesterday. The boards. The boards. When they carried him up the bank. I took the head of the boards at the lip for the last two paces. They'd have had to set him down on the stones otherwise. He swallowed. I knew I shouldn't. I knew it while I was doing it. I'd like it known that I'd do it again. I'd have done it myself, said Ask. I'd have been wrong too. He did not raise his voice. Here's the price of it, because you didn't ask for it first. A crack across a rib is a crack. A crack through is a break. And a break can go in. And in is your lung. You lifted a dead man's weight on a crack. And the strapping took it. And so did the bone. And I'm glad. It'll not take it twice. He took out his card and wrote. Standing against the window frame. Slowly, so that Perrin could read every word over his arm. Lifted against the card at the spur. Wednesday the 16th. A fortnight from Wednesday. Not from Tuesday. No plant. No lift. Nothing heavier than a cup. He capped the pen. That's one day more. I'd have given you a week more if you'd lied to me about it. Or nearly did. Oh no, you stopped. Ask to put the card away. That's why it's one day. He looked down the row. Jude was standing by the window. With his good arm on the frame. As always, looking at the sea. And his left arm hanging at his side in the sleeve of his shirt. Taily, said Ask. Your arm. It's not worse. So you've said on the boat, on the quay, at the carry and on the causeway. You've said it to everybody but me. Ask held out his hand. Roll up the sleeve. Here, in the light, where I can see it. I'll not ask a fourth time. And I'll not stand you in a lane with it on your word. Jude looked at him. Then he scratched his jaw with his right hand. And came over and sat down on Kiva's bed. And rolled up his left sleeve to the shoulder. Kiva had not seen it since the moor. She had seen the sling and the linen. And Jude holding the arm away from his side. As though it belonged to somebody else. She had not seen the arm. From the wrist to a hand's breadth below the elbow. The skin was a dull, mottled red. Shiny in places. With a dry, grey edge where the frost had stopped. Along the outside of the forearm. There was a darker stripe two fingers wide. Where something had pressed. It was not white. It was not black. It looked, Kiva thought. Like a burn that somebody had been carrying about in their pocket for a month. Asuka looked at it for a long time without touching it. Then he touched it. Very lightly. At the wrist. At the middle. And at the stripe. And watched Jude's face each time. That stripe's new. He said. The carry. The sling's loop. Two fingers. Two fingers on a frosted forearm. With eighty-five kilos of canvas and a carry hanging off it. Ask laid the arm down gently on Jude's knee. It's mending. You'll keep a mark the length of the stripe. And it'll be stiff in the cold for a year. And you'll never again be able to say it's not worse with a straight face. Because I'll know. He took out the card again. Tally. Left forearm. Frost. Mending. The edge on the right fist only. Nothing gripped with the left till Monday. He looked up. You'll fight one-handed. Can you? I've an edge on the right. Said Jude. I've always had. The left was for holding. Then hold nothing. Ask stood up. Finch. Prue held up her ten caps. Ten. Said Ask. Before he had taken one off. I know. I did them. He took the first cap off. And looked at the fingertip under it. Which was blistered. And pink. And peeling at the edge. And put the cap back on. And did the next. It took him four minutes. Nobody spoke. Dre had come back up the stair. For something she had forgotten. And stood at the head of it. Waiting for him to finish. With her face shut. Your door's in your hand. Said Ask at last. To Prue. It's not in your fingertips. You'll catch. You'll not grip a pole with those today. And if you try. You'll tear them. And then you'll not catch on Saturday either. He looked round the four of them. And at Kiva last. That's your hurt four. A captain who can't plant. A blade with one arm. A catcher who can't grip. And another with a burned hand that writes left-handed. He shut his bag. I've seen worse go into a lane. Not often. He went down the stair to his breakfast. Dre stepped aside to let him by. And then went to her bed. And took up a glove she had left on the blanket. And went down after him. Perrin sat on the end of his bed. And looked at the four of them. Well. He said. I'd hope to say something about being a team that's been tested. I'd had it ready since five. He breathed carefully. I think we'll just go and look at the drawer. Anwen Price climbed Tar Lane at eight on Thursday. With her hands in her sleeves. Because she had said tomorrow to Maud Lyle on a bench. And tomorrow had come. The rope walk's doors were open. Inside the longboards ran away under the windows. As they had on Wednesday night. Bare and black. But they were not empty now. The rope walk's first four were at the near end. In their shirt sleeves. With nobody watching. And Juniper Carrow was walking. She was not walking alone. Trine walked beside her. A pace back and to the left. With her sleeves rolled and her cord at her belt. And she was talking under her breath. Anwen could not hear the words at first. Then she could. Sit. Carrow's right foot came down. And her edge came up on her fist and stayed. She was not walking alone. Trine said nothing for three paces. Then she said it again. Set. And again Carrow's foot came down. Hard and square. And the edge lit. And Anwen understood. That she was not lighting it when she chose. She was lighting it on the word. Anwen stopped in the doorway. She had heard that word before. She had heard it from the foot of a ladder in the inner lock on Tuesday. In Kiva's voice. Flat and clear. Every time Perrin's heel came onto a rung. Set. Half of Saltmere had been standing on the lock's lip with their mouth shut. And had heard it twenty-two times. Price. I said Lyle. I said Lyle. I said Lyle. From the bench. You came. Lyle. And she felt like a cart horse. Lyle's square face did not change. She's very good at it already. She's good at everything she hates. Anwen did not say whose word it was. She thought that Caro knew perfectly well whose word it was. And that it had cost her something to take it. And that it was not Anwen's business to say so. On Caro's own floor. Show me your heels. She said instead. Lyle opened her stance. Her feet went into the boards. And Anwen felt them go. A post driven into the ridge. Sure and heavy. There was nothing at her hip. There was nothing on her hands. She stood planted in the middle of the rope walk. With her arms at her sides. And she looked. Anwen thought. Like a house with the front taken off. Lyle on me. Said Anwen. Not a wall. You. From the floor. She put her own shoulder against Lyle's. Sideways. As two people stand at a crowded rail. She did not open anything. Lyle leaned. She. Leaned from the shoulders. As people did who had always had a wall to lean with. And nothing moved. And her stance held her where she was. Like a nail holds a coat. That's from your back. Said Anwen. You're pushing with your back and holding with your feet. And the two don't know each other. That's what a wall did for you. The wall knew both. She stepped away. Again. Bend your knees. Put your weight down into the floor first. And then let the floor push. Not you. The floor. The floor. Lyle bent her knees. She put her weight down. Anwen saw it go. A long way down. Through the boards. Into the ridge. And then she saw it come back up. Slowly. Through Lyle's heels and calves and thighs. And the small of her back. Until it arrived in her shoulder. It moved Anwen half a pace. Anwen stood where she had been put. And looked at the boards between her boots. Anwen. That's it. She said. That's Laning from the floor. Lyle did not smile. Her face was white. And there was sweat at her hairline. And she was breathing as though she had run the length of the shed. But she looked at the half pace on the boards. And then at Anwen. And something went across her square, careful face. And stayed there for a moment longer than it usually did. She said. Again. She said. They did it eleven times. On the seventh, Lyle moved her a whole pace. On the ninth, Anwen stopped thinking about it. And leaned back. From her own floor. With her own heels right. The two of them stood shoulder to shoulder in the middle of the rope walk. Neither of them moving. Both of them working as hard as they could. And Anwen thought it was the strangest thing she had ever done on a lane floor. There were no doors in it at all. Except one still door. And that one was not hers. At the far end of the near boards, Caro had stopped walking. She stood with her head shut. And her hands at her sides. Watching them and Treen beside her. Price, said Caro. That's yours. That lane? It's a man called Macy's. On a van's line. At home. It's yours now. She's got it off you. Caro looked at Lyle and then back at Anwen. With her quick, blunt face giving nothing away. If the lot falls that way tomorrow. She'll lean on your four with it. You know that. I know it. And you came up the lane anyway. I said I would. Said Amwen. She asked me on a bench with her ward gone. I'd not say no to that because of a lot that hasn't been drawn. She took her hands out of her sleeves. If she leans on us tomorrow, I'll be glad she leans well. That's all. Caro considered that. In this town, she said, we'd call that daft. In mine, we'd call it the same. Said Anwen. I've been called daft before. Trine laughed. It was a short, startled sound. And she put her hand over her mouth at once. And went red under her dark skin. Caro did not laugh. But she turned her head and looked at her catcher. And something in her shoulders eased. As though Trine had called a word she had been waiting for. Sit, said Trine through her fingers. Caro's foot came down. Her edge came up. She walked on down the rope walk ten paces. And turned. And walked back. Lighting on the word. Anwen went down Tar Lane at nine. With her shoulder aching and her heels sore. She did not know whether she had done a stupid thing. She thought probably she had. She found that she did not want to have done it any other way. And that she would tell Kiva so. And that she would not tell Perrin. Who would only look pleased with her and say something kind. The drawer had gone up on the tent pole at the gate at nine the night before. Under the lamp. While the Mercury's boy was selling his late sheet on the long key. Kiva had read it then. Over the heads of a crowd in green. She read it again now. At a quarter to ten. In daylight. With Perrin at her shoulder. And the timber pond lying black and quiet under the boards. The lane. Three lanes for every four. One a day. Thursdays drawn by the standing after three boards. First against twenty-fourth. Second against twenty-third. And so down. Fridays and Saturdays. Drawn by lot at this pole at six the evening before. Winners against winners. And losers against losers. No four to meet a four twice. A four is placed by lanes one. And then by points for less points against. And marked by place. Twenty-four to the first. And one to the last. And under it. Thursdays twelve lanes. With their hours. Halden license against the twenty-fourth at nine. Old four at ten. The rope walks first four. Against the twenty-first at half past ten. In the graving. Before the whole town. And halfway down. Two o'clock. Team seven. Meridian. Against the tarn. Second four. The tarn. Said Perrin. Their second four. I know which four. I've read it nine times. He had his hand pressed to his side under his coat. Where the strapping was. Their first four's in the healer's tent. With their feet in a basin. Their second four's been watching from the tiers all week. And every one of them was on the causeway yesterday afternoon. When we came up the bank with Hebden on a stretcher. He was quiet a moment. They'll not be pleased to see us. They'll not hate us either. I'd sooner be hated. You know where you are. Beside the drawer there was a second board. Muir. That Kiva had not seen the night before. It was a plain deal board on two trestles. With a strip of green baize along its top. And a row of brass drawing pins. Somebody had chalked across the head of it. In a big, careful hand. Draft. Cards may be put up by any chartered company. And taken down by the student named. A card is not a seat. There were already eleven cards on it. Kiva did not go close. She saw Jude go close. He went past her without seeming to see her. With the book under his good arm. And stood in front of the board for a long time. Reading one card near the middle. In the company's green. Then he put out his right hand. And touched the card's corner. As a man touches the edge of a table in the dark. He did not take it down. He came back with his face very still. And the book under his arm. Taly. Said Perrin. I'll write it again tonight. Said Jude. It's not going anywhere. He walked on toward the graving. Perrin looked after him. And then at the board. And then. Very carefully. Not at the two cards in the bottom corner. That had Cade P. Written on them. In two different hands. The graving was half full at two. Which was full enough. It was not. The rope walks lane. And the town knew it. The rope walk had beaten the twenty-first. At half past ten. Seven to nothing. In front of every tier in the dock. The green had gone home to its dinner. And come back slowly. A few at a time. And it sat now in the lower tiers. In the grey light from the glass roof. Eating pasties. And talking about the morning. The tarns brown and buff. Sat in a knot near the middle. Meridian's colours were above them. Orla was there on the end of a tier. With ask beside her. Rea Saan sat two tiers higher with Pike. Whose hands lay on his knees. Closed halfway. Down on the floor. Eighty feet below the lip. The pen was chalked on the stone. Twenty paces wide. With its hurdles and its posts. And its seven chalk squares. On its north side. Between the pen and the dock wall. The board had stood a mast. It was not as tall as the gate mast. It came up to a drum. At about twice a man's height. With eight pens on eight wires. And two reading desks at its foot. Noah stood at one. With his pencil behind his ear. Polgley stood at the other. In his steel spectacles. Threading tape. Perrin declared at the marshal's box. He did not go into the pen. He stood behind Seven's hurdle in his coat. With his hands at his sides. And his voice came up the dock's stone walls. Clear and flat. Team Seven. Price. Ward. Tally. Edge. Finch. Ward. Catcher. Rowan. Stance. Declared. By her captain's voice. Cade. Captain. Standing out on his healer's card. There was a murmur round the tears. Standing out. Kiva heard it go round and come back. And she let it go past her. She was looking at the tarn's second floor. Coming out of the dock's side door. In brown and buff. They were big. They were big. Everybody from the tarn was big. As if the hills grew them on purpose. Their captain was a thin dark girl with a still door. Who walked as though the stone under her were a field she knew. The others came behind her. A heavy blade. A hold with long arms. A catcher with a fresh bandage on one wrist. They stood behind their hurdle. And looked down the pen at seven. And Kiva saw them look at the linen on her right hand. And Prue's ten caps. And Jude's left arm hanging. And Perrin standing outside the pen with his hand pressed to his side. Their captain looked longest at Perrin. Then she looked at Kiva. And inclined her head an inch. It was the same nod Truen gave. Done properly. She was on the causeway. Said Anwen very low. Yesterday. She carried one end of Hebden's stretcher to the tent. I know. Said Kiva. Declared. Said the marshal. Ready. He turned his glass. The first carry showed them what they could not do. They had made the plan at the long table at eleven. On Perrin's slate. With Perrin drawing it and nobody else allowed to touch the chalk. It was a plain plan. Kiva would plant at the head of the litter with her stance. And nobody could shift it while she stood there. Anwen's wall would go up on the south side. Jude would take the north with his edge on his right fist. Prue would stand back of the litter with her ward low and her eyes on hands and call. When the moment came, Anwen and Jude would lift and walk the Commodore home. And Kiva would shut and run ahead to the hurdle. And she and Prue would take it over from the far side. Two to two. Top to top. It went well until the hurdle. The tarn came in a square. As the first four had come against Prue in the seeding lane. Their hold's wall met Anwen's with the sound of a shut drawer. And the two walls leaned. And Anwen's heels were right. And the tarns were not. And Anwen walked her wall from the far end round in a quarter circle. While the other girl was still leaning. Prue called hands south off the tarn blade's fingers. And Jude was there. And the tarn blade stopped short of his edge. Kiva stood planted at the litter's head. With her stance in the stone and her hands on nothing. Nobody tried to shift her. Nobody wasted the time. Now, said Prue. Anwen and Jude lifted. Anwen had both hands on the head poles. And Jude had his right hand on the foot. With his left arm held against his chest. And the commodore came up. Crooked. Heavy at the foot. And they walked him. Kiva shut her stance and ran. She vaulted Seven's hurdle. And turned on the far side. As Carrow had turned in the rope walk. And put up her hands for the head. Her right hand would not close. She had known it would not. She had known it at the table. At eleven. With the chalk in Perrin's fist. And set it. And Perrin had said wrist then. And she had said wrist. But a wrist under a pole is not a hand round it. And the head of the commodore came over the hazel at her. And she took it on her left hand. And her right wrist. And it went down on the right. Prue had the foot. Prue had put her capped fingers round the foot poles. Because that was where the foot was. Commodore's foot went down on the hazel. Touched. Touched. Touched. Said the marshal. Dropped. Anybody's. It was the tarns. Their still door was there before Kiva had got her wrist out from under. And their hold behind her. And they walked the commodore away from Seven's hurdle. As though it had been left out for them. Jude got a half on the hold's arm as she turned. It was not enough. The tarn blade touched Anwen on the shoulder as she came round her own wall. Quite gently. And Anwen knelt. The glass ran out with the commodore lying across the middle line on the tarn side of it. A down to the tarn. A point to the tarn by the half. Said the marshal. Two to the tarn. Nothing to seven. The tears made the warm sound. Not loud. Kiva stood on the far side of her own hurdle with her right hand held against her chest. The blisters under the linen had opened. She could feel them wet. Prue was standing beside her. With her hands held up in front of her face. Two of the caps had come off on the paws. The fingertips under them were bleeding a little. Don't. Don't say you're sorry. I wasn't going to. Prue's face was white, not scarlet. I was going to say that I can't grip and you can't grip and that's half our hands and we've two more carries. She looked at the bleeding fingertips with a sort of fury. Asky said. He said you'll tear them. I tore them. Perrin had come to the hurdle from the outside. He stood with his hands on the hazel.
